A Bloomberg report pointed out that Apple shareholders have reaped remarkable returns during Tim Cook's tenure as CEO, with cumulative gains reaching 2,275%, and a total return of 2,736% when including dividends.

The website believes Cook has set a standard that is difficult to surpass, but the author believes that the new CEO, John Ternus, does not need to follow the way Cook managed the company...

The figures cited by Bloomberg are indisputable.

However, the author believes John Ternus need not worry at all about whether Apple can continue to deliver the same level of financial success under his leadership, for two reasons.

First, both of his main predecessors held the view that financial results are a by-product of the real goal, not something that should be pursued directly. Steve Jobs famously said:

Cook himself has also echoed this philosophy, saying he never worries about quarterly results, but focuses on the company's long-term direction.

Second, there is the advice Steve gave when he passed the baton to Tim:

Ternus does not need to ask himself what Jobs or Cook would have done, but rather should run Apple in the way that he believes is most likely to succeed in developing the best products and shaping the most ideal corporate culture and values, thereby achieving long-term success.

I expect him to be a very different CEO from Cook, just as Cook was different from Jobs. The point is not to try to emulate past formulas for success, but to look to the future — to borrow a phrase from this outgoing CEO — and follow your own North Star.

Do you agree with my view, or do you have a different perspective? Feel free to tell us your thoughts in the comments section.
